title: NVIDIA NVLink Fusion Brings NVHBM to Next-Generation AI Infrastructure | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA is positioning NVLink Fusion (interconnect IP) and NVHBM (custom HBM base-die technology) as the way it keeps capturing value even as hyperscalers and AI-native companies build their own custom XPU accelerators, by making its scale-up/scale-out fabric and rack architecture (MGX) the mandatory substrate those chips plug into.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's NVLink Fusion is explicitly designed to let hyperscalers and AI-native companies deploy their own custom XPU and CPU accelerators inside NVIDIA's AI infrastructure platform, meaning NVIDIA can still monetize infrastructure IP, interconnect, and rack architecture even when a customer's compute silicon is not an NVIDIA GPU.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: This is NVIDIA's structural hedge against the custom-ASIC threat (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA) — even if hyperscalers succeed in cutting NVIDIA GPU spend, NVIDIA can still capture economics via NVLink Fusion licensing, NVHBM IP, and MGX rack architecture, defending its moat at the platform/interconnect layer rather than the chip layer.
insights.quote: NVIDIA NVLink Fusion is the connective technology and IP that enables hyperscalers and AI natives to deploy custom XPUs and CPUs into the NVIDIA AI infrastructure platform.

insights.claim: NVIDIA describes the resulting products built with NVLink Fusion and NVHBM as 'semi-custom AI factories,' implying a business model where NVIDIA supplies the standardized connective and memory IP layer while customers retain design control of the compute die itself.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: This 'semi-custom' framing is a category NVIDIA is trying to own — akin to how AMD/console makers do semi-custom silicon — positioning NVIDIA as the indispensable infrastructure vendor across both merchant GPU and custom-XPU markets simultaneously.
insights.locator: closing section 'The next phase of custom AI silicon'

insights.claim: By standardizing NVLink Fusion as a single unified architecture across GPUs and custom XPUs, NVIDIA enables customers to mix heterogeneous compute (its own GPUs alongside third-party XPUs) in the same rack and to flexibly reprovision data center capacity across workloads.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous compute support reduces the switching cost hyperscalers face when diversifying away from pure NVIDIA GPU fleets, which paradoxically increases the odds customers adopt custom XPUs sooner — but locks that mixed fleet into NVIDIA's fabric and software stack regardless.
insights.quote: By standardizing on a single unified architecture, NVLink Fusion simplifies operations across the data center, enables flexible reprovisioning of data center capacity, and enables custom AI XPUs to integrate with GPUs for heterogeneous compute.
insights.locator: section 'Combining NVLink Fusion with NVHBM at rack scale'

insights.claim: NVHBM, NVIDIA's custom HBM base-die technology co-designed and validated with leading memory vendors, delivers up to 30% more memory bandwidth per stack than standard HBM4e.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Higher per-stack bandwidth directly raises usable throughput for memory-bound inference/training workloads, meaning XPU partners get GPU-competitive memory performance without needing NVIDIA's own compute die — a value-add NVIDIA is selling as IP.
insights.quote: NVHBM delivers up to 30% more memory bandwidth per stack compared with standard HBM4e.
insights.locator: section 'The memory bandwidth bottleneck in modern AI accelerators'

insights.claim: NVHBM reduces PHY and support area by up to 67% versus the JEDEC HBM4e standard by moving the memory controller into the 3D HBM stack and integrating a custom PHY, freeing up to 30% more main-die silicon for compute or added features.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: For custom-XPU designers, area is a direct proxy for either more compute (better performance/TCO) or lower die cost — NVHBM effectively lets a hyperscaler's custom chip pack more logic in the same reticle-limited package, a concrete economic lever NVIDIA is licensing.
insights.quote: Compared with the JEDEC HBM4e standard, this design reduces PHY and support area by up to 67%.

insights.claim: NVHBM cuts HBM power consumption by up to 15% versus standard HBM4e, and NVIDIA calculates this could support roughly 15,000 additional XPUs (at 2,000W each) of compute headroom within a fixed 1-gigawatt data center power budget.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: This quantifies power, not chip supply, as the binding constraint on AI factory scale-out — a memory-level power efficiency gain translates directly into more deployable compute per gigawatt of grid capacity, which is increasingly the scarcest input in AI infrastructure buildouts.
insights.quote: When compounded across an entire 1-gigawatt data center using 2,000W XPUs, power savings can enable up to 15,000 additional XPUs in compute headroom.

insights.claim: Combining NVLink Fusion connectivity with NVHBM's bandwidth, area, and power gains compounds into a claimed 30% overall end-to-end performance increase per XPU at rack scale.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is quantifying the value of its 'full stack' (interconnect + memory IP + rack architecture) as a bundled 30% performance uplift — the pitch to hyperscalers is that going custom-silicon without NVIDIA's platform leaves that performance on the table.
insights.quote: these co-designed architectural improvements translate into a significant 30% overall end-to-end performance increase per XPU.
insights.locator: section 'Combining NVLink Fusion with NVHBM at rack scale'

insights.claim: Faster HBM access under NVHBM is credited with speeding KV-cache reads, which the article says increases per-user token throughput during large-model inference.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Inference economics (tokens/sec/user, cost per token) are increasingly the metric investors should track for AI infrastructure ROI; memory bandwidth improvements at the component level are a lever hyperscalers can pull to improve inference unit economics independent of buying new GPUs.
insights.quote: This can increase per-user token throughput during large-model inference by moving data between HBM and compute cores faster, keeping them fed.
insights.locator: section 'The memory bandwidth bottleneck in modern AI accelerators'

insights.claim: NVLink is now in its sixth generation and is described by NVIDIA as 'the only proven, purpose-built scale-up networking fabric for AI factories,' explicitly connecting all XPUs in a rack into a single scale-up domain via the NVLink Fusion chiplet.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: This is a direct competitive claim against alternative scale-up fabrics (e.g., UALink, proprietary hyperscaler interconnects) — NVIDIA is betting its moat now sits more in the interconnect/fabric layer (six generations of maturity) than in the GPU die itself, which is the layer least likely to be displaced quickly even as compute diversifies.
insights.quote: Now in its sixth generation, NVLink is the only proven, purpose-built scale-up networking fabric for AI factories, delivering leading performance and intelligent resiliency.
insights.locator: section 'Combining NVLink Fusion with NVHBM at rack scale'

insights.claim: NVLink is described as critical for advanced routing techniques like expert parallelism (EP) and WideEP, where different experts reside on different GPUs and require high-speed synchronization of activations and hidden states across the entire rack.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: As MoE architectures become standard for frontier models, the scale-up fabric (not just raw GPU FLOPs) becomes a binding constraint on serving performance — this reinforces why NVIDIA is pushing NVLink Fusion adoption even for non-NVIDIA compute dies, to keep the fabric layer as the chokepoint.
insights.locator: section 'The memory bandwidth bottleneck in modern AI accelerators'
